fact_checks.fact: The team led by Nandita Saha tested the new MRI antenna by imaging the eye and orbit in volunteers using a 7.0 Tesla MRI scanner. Traditional MRI antennas, known as RF coils, often have trouble collecting enough signal from tissues located deep inside the body or in anatomically complex regions. Even with today's advanced scanners, producing clear images of some areas remains difficult. The project brought together experts in MRI physics, clinical ophthalmology, and translational imaging from the Max Delbrück Center and Rostock University Medical Center. The team led by Nandita Saha is preparing larger clinical studies involving multiple hospitals while modifying the new MRI antenna for additional organs, including the heart and kidneys. A team led by Nandita Saha, a doctoral student in Professor Thoralf Niendorf's Experimental Ultrahigh Field Magnetic Resonance laboratory at the Max Delbrück Center, has developed a new MRI antenna based on advanced engineered materials.
